title: Probing Whether Activation-Based Jailbreak Detectors Generalize Across Attack Types

original_idea.problem: Whether a probe trained on one attack class also detects other attack classes is not known.
original_idea.direction: Train a linear probe on one attack class (GCG). Test zero-shot on 2-3 other attack classes (prefilling, multi-turn, role-play). Measure AUROC per class.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If probes are attack-type-specific, defenders need separate probes per class. If they generalize, a single cheap probe suffices.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: cross-attack generalization -> determines deployment viability of single-probe defense -> directly affects cost and feasibility of activation-based safety.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction, linear probe training, and testing across attack types. Intermediate complexity. Dataset preparation across attack types adds overhead.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: cross-attack AUROC table. Train one probe, test on multiple classes. Clear methodology with a well-defined output.

novelty.reasoning: Cross-attack generalization of jailbreak probes is a known open question. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) found that single-layer probes have limited ability to classify successful jailbreaking prompts from held-out attack methods, suggesting different attacks use different features. 'Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?' (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop) uses tensor decomposition for cross-attack detection. However, the specific experimental design — train on GCG, test zero-shot on prefilling, multi-turn, and role-play, report AUROC per class — has not been systematically published with this exact protocol. The question is partially addressed but the clean cross-attack transfer matrix remains a novel experimental contribution.
